title: Saga pattern
summary: Transactions across microservices without two-phase commit: local commits, compensations in reverse, choreography vs orchestration, and the isolation a saga gives up.

clips.title: Why not two-phase commit?
clips.question: An order spans payment, inventory and shipping services. Why not use two-phase commit?

scenes.say: Saga, question one. One order spans the payment, inventory and shipping services. Why not wrap it in a two-phase commit? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: One order, three services. Why not two-phase commit?

scenes.say: Two-phase commit makes every service prepare, and hold its locks, until a coordinator says commit. It is strongly consistent, but one slow or failed participant blocks everyone, and the coordinator becomes a single point of failure. A saga commits each step locally, right away. If a later step fails, it undoes the completed steps with compensating transactions. Higher availability and no long-held locks, in exchange for only eventual consistency.

props.title: Lock and wait, or commit and compensate

left.label: Two-phase commit
left.title: Lock, then commit
left.body: Strongly consistent, but participants hold locks until the coordinator decides. One slow service blocks all.

right.label: Saga
right.title: Commit, then compensate
right.body: Each step commits locally at once; failures trigger compensating transactions, in reverse.

verdict.text: Sagas trade isolation and instant consistency for availability.

clips.title: Compensating in reverse
clips.question: Payment and inventory succeeded, then shipping fails. What does the saga do?

scenes.say: Question two. In an order saga, payment and inventory have already committed, and then shipping fails. What happens next? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Shipping fails after payment and inventory committed. Now what?

scenes.say: An orchestrator runs the order saga as a sequence of local transactions. First it creates the order, in a pending state. Payment charges the card, and commits locally. Inventory reserves the stock. Then shipping fails: no courier is available. There is no global rollback, so the orchestrator runs compensating transactions, in reverse order. Inventory releases the stock. Payment refunds the card. And the order is marked cancelled. Every compensation must be idempotent, because it may be retried.

steps.note: No global rollback: compensate in reverse
Undo 1: order CANCELLED · compensations are idempotent

clips.title: Choreography, orchestration, isolation
clips.question: Choreography or orchestration, and what does a saga give up?

scenes.say: Question three. Should services choreograph the saga with events, or should an orchestrator drive it? And what does a saga give up compared with a database transaction? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Choreography or orchestration, and what does a saga give up?

scenes.say: Two ways to run it. In choreography, each service listens for the previous service's event, and emits its own. There is no central piece, but the flow is spread across every service, and hard to follow. In orchestration, a central state machine sends commands, and records progress. It is easier to reason about and debug, at the cost of one more service to run.

left.label: Choreography
left.title: React to events
left.body: Loosely coupled, no central piece, but the flow is implicit and cycles creep in.

right.label: Orchestration
right.title: Central state machine
right.body: Explicit flow, easy to trace and debug; one more service to operate.

verdict.text: More than two or three steps: orchestrate.

scenes.say: A saga has no isolation: another request can see the half-finished order. Countermeasures: a semantic lock, like a pending status that other flows respect. Commutative updates, which can apply in any order. And step ordering: put the risky steps before the pivot, the point after which the saga always runs to completion. Finally, make every compensation idempotent.

items.label: Semantic lock
items.title: PENDING status
items.body: Other flows see and respect in-progress work.

items.label: Updates
items.title: Commutative
items.body: Increments and decrements apply in any order.

items.label: Ordering
items.title: Risky first
items.body: After the pivot step, only retryable steps remain.

scenes.say: To recap. A saga replaces one distributed transaction with local commits. A failure triggers compensating transactions, in reverse order. Orchestration keeps the flow explicit. And without isolation, use semantic locks, careful ordering, and idempotent compensations.

items.text: Local commits instead of one distributed transaction.
No isolation: semantic locks, idempotent undo.
